quotes.text: The real problem is that your clean up can't run itself again, so every new file drags you back to the same manual steps.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes data cleanup as a repeatability problem rather than a messy-data problem.

quotes.text: The manual cleanup lives in your memory and disappears when you close the file, while the recorded one waits for you and runs again on demand.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear contrast between manual cleanup and recorded Power Query steps.

quotes.text: The simplest way to hold on to the difference is this merge makes your table wider and append makes it longer

quotes.text: When your source is a database, Power Query can push supported transformations back to that database and let it do the heavy lifting, which is often far faster than pulling everything into Power Query first.

takeaways: Power Query is the data transformation engine built into Excel, Power BI and other Microsoft tools, and every click becomes a recorded, replayable step.
The workflow follows four phases—connect, transform, combine and load—and refresh reruns the saved steps without changing the source data.
Setting data types (with locale) early, filtering at the top and understanding query folding keep queries correct and fast.
hook: If you clean the same spreadsheet by hand every month, Power Query can turn that ritual into a process that repeats itself. This beginner-friendly episode explains the four phases, applied steps, the M language, merge versus append and the habits that keep queries fast, for Excel and Power BI users who want to stop doing manual cleanup.
